title: All (ordinary) optimizers work with arbitrary degrees of freedom
body:
This MR parametrizes the test that verifies that an optimizer on a "pure" (analytic) function in 2D.  Now we test all eligible (ordinary gradient based) optimizers.

It also fixes all the array shapes in all the optimizers.  (Only BFGS was working previously)

The optimizer step() implementations now ~~ignore the forces argument~~ convert the existing `forces` to flat gradients (and issue a warning so we can remove the `step(forces)` argument).  Although arguably *better* for performance to pass the forces if they were available, I didn't want to fight both the implementations and their callers at the same time.  As it turned out, we almost never pass the forces to step().  So maybe this will not be a huge performance hit.

# Checklist: `x` (done) or `~` (irrelevant)

comments.author: ajjackson
comments.body:
The internal logic is getting cleaner, which is lovely to see! The Booth function test across all optimizers is also a very nice thing to have, and in not too many lines of code :smile: 

My main concern is the API breakage that removes the `f` parameter from all optimize `step()` methods. This is a public method and there is a real possibility someone is using this to do some kind of hack around optimization.

I wonder if it would be prudent to
- mark this a **breaking** in the changelog, and
- raise an *Error* if the argument is used so that workflows do not start producing incorrect results "quietly".

Ideally those users would also be provided some other way to achieve whatever it was they were doing: perhaps this is supported by documenting some examples of custom Optimizeable.

I recently tried to make a filter-like Optimizeable (which presents a primitive cell but calculates a supercell) and found it a bit cumbersome to apply. Perhaps we can use that starting-point to find or create a reasonably streamlined example in the docs.

review_threads.actionability_reasoning: Requests multiple concrete changes: marking the changelog as breaking, raising an Error on deprecated argument use, documenting examples of custom Optimizeable, and potentially adding a streamlined example in the docs.

comments.author: ajjackson
comments.body:
A slightly cumbersome but fair-to-end-users solution to gradient/force sign conventions might involve an optional `negative=True` parameter on `get_gradient()` which
- defaults to existing behaviour (i.e. wrong sign)
- is explicitly corrected to new convention internally (i.e. all internal calls to `get_gradient` are `get_gradient(negative=False)`
- raises deprecation warning if used with default

- Then later we change the default and raise an error if you try to use the old behaviour
- Then later remove the parameter

`Optimizable.get_gradient()` is in a release so we shouldn't just invert the behaviour overnight! But because we have warned that Optimizable is a bit experimental this could be done a bit more swiftly than typical deprecations.

review_threads.actionability_reasoning: Proposes a concrete, detailed deprecation strategy for the gradient/force sign convention, including a specific API change (`negative` parameter), migration steps, and a phased removal plan.

comments.author: askhl
comments.body:
> My main concern is the API breakage that removes the `f` parameter from all optimize `step()` methods. This is a public method and there is a real possibility someone is using this to do some kind of hack around optimization.

Most algorithms get the forces many times in different places.  So I think `step(my_own_forces)` simply doesn't work for most optimizers.  I have nevertheless changed the `_ignored()` method to something that flattens the input forces and issues a warning.

(Note that the parameter wasn't *removed*, it was just ignored but with a warning.)

> mark this a **breaking** in the changelog

Maybe not necessary now?

We want to flip the sign, too (right now gradients are still actually the forces), so there will be more shenanigans after this MR.

> I recently tried to make a filter-like Optimizeable (which presents a primitive cell but calculates a supercell) and found it a bit cumbersome to apply. Perhaps we can use that starting-point to find or create a reasonably streamlined example in the docs.

It would be interesting to see that example.  Maybe we need an explicit "convert between dumb gradients and domain data (forces/stresses etc.)" step?

> This could be a problem for ASE4, if the new "functional" calculators do not cache forces?

The current situation is not significantly different from how things always were.
